summary:
Exodus continues Genesis directly: "These are the names of the sons of Israel who went to Egypt with Jacob" (1:1) — the line behind its Hebrew title, Shemot, "Names"; "Exodus" is Greek for "departure." Jacob's seventy have grown into a nation, and "a new king, who did not know Joseph" (1:8) forces them into slave labor and orders their newborn boys drowned. The text never names this Pharaoh, and the date is debated: the figure in 1 Kings 6:1 works out to the mid-1400s BC, while the store city "Rameses" (1:11) leads many scholars to the 1200s BC. The book moves in three stages: deliverance from Egypt (chapters 1–15), covenant at Sinai (16–24), and the tabernacle (25–40).

Moses survives the drowning decree in a papyrus basket on the Nile — the Hebrew word, tevah, is the one Genesis uses for Noah's ark — and is raised by Pharaoh's daughter, kills an Egyptian overseer, and flees to Midian. There God speaks from a bush "ablaze with fire, but it was not consumed" (3:2) and gives His name: "I AM WHO I AM" (3:14; Hebrew ehyeh asher ehyeh), tied to the name rendered "the LORD" in English Bibles. Moses' demand, "Let My people go" (5:1), is refused, and ten plagues follow, from the Nile turned to blood to the death of every firstborn, a night God calls "judgment against all the gods of Egypt" (12:12). Israel escapes it by the first Passover: each household marks its doorframes with a lamb's blood — "when I see the blood, I will pass over you" (12:13) — and the meal becomes an annual feast; the New Testament applies it to Jesus ("Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed," 1 Corinthians 5:7). At the sea the water divides, and Israel walks through on "dry ground, with walls of water on their right and on their left" (14:22) while Pharaoh's army drowns behind them. The Hebrew name, yam suph, is traditionally translated "Red Sea," though many scholars render it "Sea of Reeds," and the crossing's location is debated.

In the wilderness God feeds the people with manna, named for their question "What is it?" (16:15), and in the third month they camp at Mount Sinai (19:1). God offers a covenant, a formal oath-bound pact patterned on ancient treaties: if Israel obeys, "you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations" and "a kingdom of priests and a holy nation" (19:5–6). The Ten Commandments open with the rescue already accomplished: "I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery" (20:2). Case laws follow (chapters 21–23), and in chapter 24 the covenant is sealed with sacrificial blood and a meal before God on the mountain.

Chapters 25–31 give instructions for the tabernacle (Hebrew mishkan, "dwelling place"), a portable tent-sanctuary: "make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them" (25:8). While Moses is still on the mountain, Aaron casts a golden calf and the people declare, "These, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!" (32:4). Moses shatters the tablets, then intercedes, and the covenant is remade; God proclaims His own character in a line the rest of the Old Testament keeps quoting (Numbers 14:18; Psalm 103:8; Jonah 4:2): "The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness" (34:6), yet One who "will by no means leave the guilty unpunished" (34:7).

Chapters 35–40 build it all to specification — "Moses did everything just as the LORD had commanded him" (40:16) — and the book ends with the sanctuary put to its stated use: "Then the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle" (40:34), so completely that even Moses cannot enter (40:35). The last verse leaves Israel mid-journey, the cloud over the tabernacle by day and fire in it by night, "in the sight of all the house of Israel through all their journeys" (40:38).
